summary: Harris Wittels joins David Choe, Asa Akira, Money Mark, Critter, Valentin, and Bobby Namba for an episode that moves from television comedy and the invention of “humblebrag” into one of the corpus's clearest contemporaneous records of active opioid dependence. Harris describes writing for The Sarah Silverman Program at twenty-two, Parks and Recreation, and Eastbound & Down; his Humblebrag Twitter feed and book have made it difficult to speak about his own success without being accused of the behavior he named. David recounts meeting Harris in Hawaii while on a pass from gambling rehab: a proposed HBO series based on David brought Harris there to collect stories, and their first outing involved Filet-O-Fish sandwiches, spray paint, and unauthorized Munko drawings. They debate whether any topic is permissible in comedy, with a recent Boston Marathon bombing joke and Michael Richards's Laugh Factory rant as controls; the editorial layer preserves the argument without treating laughter as a universal harm waiver. The center begins when sexual discussion reveals Harris had used Vicodin, OxyContin, oxycodone, and Norco. Harris openly says he is currently dependent, describes tolerance and rationalizations around work, and says he wants to quit while repeatedly postponing it. David compares this with gambling addiction, offers treatment, warns that a functioning addiction is only functioning until it is not, and later says he is watching Harris's health and career crumble. The room also circulates unsafe lay claims about relative addictiveness, dosing, tapering, abrupt cessation, and substituting work, exercise, sex, or food; none is medical guidance. A later-history note belongs beside, not inside, this 2013 testimony: Harris subsequently spoke publicly about heroin addiction and rehab and died in 2015, while his sister Stephanie Wittels Wachs later documented the family's experience in Everything Is Horrible and Wonderful. The episode should not reduce Harris to that outcome. It also captures his craft, wit, love of Phish, appetite, television work, and ability to make “humblebrag” a precise comic tool. David's long rehab account examines celebrity exceptions, exploitative requests, relapse, substitute compulsion, institutional gratitude and resentment, and the limits of rescuing friends. Separate sections cover David's proposed self-published books, Harris's work stories, stand-up, luxury toro at Urasawa, and the conflict between making art and feeding compulsions. Trivia moves through Emily VanCamp, Blink-182, Temple of the Dog, Chris Cornell, and Eddie Vedder before Harris's introduction to Aubrey Plaza closes the interview. Seven empty cleaner drops are safe, fifty contextual corrections materially improve the text, and 2,478 identity windows are intact. Named dialogue remains withheld.

works: Humblebrag: The Art of False Modesty

connections.label: Humblebrag becomes a trap for its inventor
connections.note: Harris coined a precise term for disguised boasting, built a feed and book around it, then found every truthful statement about his career classified as the same behavior. Naming a social pattern also made him permanently answerable to it.

connections.label: Harris's craft must precede the tragedy
connections.note: The episode documents a working writer across Sarah Silverman, Parks and Recreation, Eastbound & Down, stand-up, music fandom, and a successful comic concept. Addiction is central evidence, but it is not the whole person or the only index route.

connections.label: A proposed television show creates the friendship
connections.note: Scott Rudin's interest and an HBO possibility send Harris to Hawaii to gather David's stories. The project does not materialize here, but the research trip produces a durable personal relationship.

connections.label: Rehab rules bend around celebrity
connections.note: David describes anonymity, visitor, money, and pass rules changing once staff learned who he was. The exceptions provide access and opportunity while undermining the equal-treatment container the program claimed to provide.

connections.label: Funny is not a universal harm waiver
connections.note: Harris and David argue every subject can be available if the joke succeeds, while Michael Richards's rant serves as a failed control. Editorially, humor can explain intent and form but cannot erase targets, context, or consequences.

connections.label: This is contemporaneous addiction evidence
connections.note: Harris states current OxyContin dependence, increased use, abstaining for the recording, desire to quit, and repeated postponement. These are his June 2013 words, not a diagnosis reconstructed after his death.

connections.label: Work is both protection and rationalization
connections.note: Harris says constant writing keeps him functional and busy, then uses scripts and deadlines to defer stopping. Creative productivity can coexist with serious dependence and make deterioration harder to recognize.

connections.label: Functioning describes a phase, not safety
connections.note: David compares Harris's opioid use with his own gambling: both remain outwardly manageable until escalation removes the margin. The observation is experiential, not a clinical prognosis.

connections.label: The room contains unsafe treatment talk
connections.note: Participants compare OxyContin with heroin, discuss doses, guess withdrawal timing, and recommend tapering or abrupt cessation. The transcript preserves historical speech; the reader must clearly state that none is individualized medical advice.

connections.label: Replacement compulsion links the archive
connections.note: Exercise, work, sex, food, skydiving, and painting are all proposed as substitutes for opioids or gambling. The episode recognizes transfer without distinguishing healthy routine, intense interest, and clinically harmful compulsion.

connections.label: David moves between care and control
connections.note: He offers treatment and correctly recognizes readiness cannot be forced, but also stages the public conversation, predicts collapse, and repeatedly frames friends as people he must rescue. Care is genuine and boundary-blurred.

connections.label: Later history belongs in a separate layer
connections.note: Harris later discussed heroin addiction and rehab publicly and died in 2015. Stephanie Wittels Wachs's Everything Is Horrible and Wonderful documents the family's experience. Those facts contextualize the archive but must not rewrite what anyone knew in 2013.

connections.label: Recovery institutions can help and exploit
connections.note: David credits the Hawaii program with stopping his gambling while alleging celebrity exceptions, unwanted asks, and dependency from peers and staff. Gratitude and criticism are not mutually exclusive, but individual testimony is not a comprehensive efficacy audit.

connections.label: Self-publishing extends David's control problem
connections.note: Book construction turns into a debate about rights, structure, manufacturing, shipping, and publishers. The desire to own the object resembles his insistence on controlling painting, podcast, and life-story adaptations.

connections.label: Luxury food recreates the fast reward
connections.note: Toro at Urasawa, a thousand-dollar meal, and the imagined Filet-O-Fish substitution turn appetite into immediate intensity. David explicitly contrasts that fast event with the slow process of making and selling a painting.

connections.label: The fuzzy queue fails on a recurring character
connections.note: It proposes changing four instances of Stevie to Steve-O. Every occurrence is Stevie Janowski from Eastbound & Down, demonstrating that string similarity without episode context would corrupt a central television connection.

connections.label: Trivia preserves wrong answers as process
connections.note: Calista Flockhart and Mike Watt are audible guesses; Emily VanCamp, Chris Cornell, and Eddie Vedder supply the resolved answers. The editorial layer corrects entities without falsifying the game's memory failures.

connections.label: Text confidence and speaker confidence remain separate
connections.note: Episode Thirty-One has strong text, seven safe empty-only cleaner drops, and 2,478 fixed-window identity embeddings. It still lacks independently validated multi-speaker naming, so people remain episode metadata rather than dialogue labels.
